slides.title: How a network remembers
slides.body:
**Recurrent neural networks, in motion**

Pavel Kordík · NI-MVI, FIT CTU in Prague

![[fig-rnn-cover|128%]]
slides.notes: Today one idea, in motion: a network that carries something from one word to the next. Everything else — LSTMs, the trouble with long sentences, even why recurrence is back in fashion — follows from that loop.
slides.summary: A fly-through of the one idea behind recurrent networks — a state carried from word to word — and of what came of it: training through time, why it forgets, the LSTM's gates, attention, and the comeback of recurrence.

slides.title: A feed-forward network has no yesterday
slides.body:
![[fig-rnn-ff|128%]]

> Language arrives in order, and the order matters.
slides.notes: Feed a sentence to an ordinary network one word at a time and watch: each word goes in, a guess comes out, and nothing stays. 'The' after 'sat on' and 'The' at the start get the same answer. For language that is hopeless — what a word means depends on what came before it.
slides.summary: A feed-forward network sees one word at a time and keeps nothing between them, so the same word always gets the same guess whatever came before it; language needs memory.

slides.title: Add a loop: the state
slides.notes: The fix is one arrow. Whatever the cell computed — we call it h, the state — goes back in with the next word. Two weight matrices: W for the new word, U for what we carried. The bars on the right are h: a handful of numbers that every word nudges.
slides.summary: The recurrent cell adds a loop: its output h, the state, goes back in together with the next word, h_t = tanh(W x_t + U h_{t−1} + b); the state is a vector that every word changes.

slides.title: Unrolled in time: one cell, copied
slides.body:
![[fig-rnn-unroll|128%]]

> One cell, the same weights, as many steps as the sentence is long.
slides.notes: Draw the loop out in time and it becomes a chain. It is not five networks — it is one cell, the same W and U, used five times. That is why it takes a sentence of any length, and it is also the picture we need for training.
slides.summary: Unrolling the loop shows the recurrent network as one cell copied along time, the state handed from copy to copy; every copy shares the weights W and U, so the network handles a sentence of any length.

slides.title: What the state holds
slides.body:
![[fig-rnn-state|128%]]

> Trained to predict the next word, a unit learns to wait for the verb.
slides.notes: So what does h hold? Nobody tells it. Train it only to predict the next word, and look inside: most units flicker with every word, but some hold one fact for as long as it matters. 'The keys to the cabinet are' — the network has to remember 'keys' is plural across 'cabinet'. Linzen and colleagues showed LSTMs doing exactly that; Karpathy found cells that track open quotes.
slides.summary: What is in the state: after training, most units change with every word, but some keep one fact for as long as it matters — Linzen, Dupoux and Goldberg (2016) found LSTMs tracking whether the subject is plural across 'the keys to the cabinet … are'; Karpathy (2015) showed units that track quotes and brackets.

slides.title: Learning: backpropagation through time
slides.body:
![[fig-rnn-bptt|128%]]

> Blame is passed back step by step — and every step multiplies it.
slides.notes: To learn, we use the chain we just drew. Run forward, measure the error at the end, and send the blame back through every step — backpropagation through time. Look at the numbers: each step back multiplies the gradient by another factor.
slides.summary: Training unrolls the network and sends the error back through every step (backpropagation through time, Werbos 1990); the gradient reaching step t is a product of one factor per step in between.

slides.title: Why it forgets: vanishing and exploding gradients
slides.body:
![[fig-rnn-vanish|128%]]

> Thirty steps back, the signal is gone — or it is everything.
slides.notes: Multiply by 0.9 thirty times and you have four per cent left; by 1.1 and you have seventeen times as much. That is the whole problem with plain RNNs: the error from a word thirty steps away either vanishes or blows up. Hochreiter saw it in 1991, Bengio and colleagues in 1994. Clipping tames the explosion; the vanishing needs a new cell.
slides.summary: Multiplying by roughly the same factor at every step makes the gradient vanish when the factor is below one and explode when it is above (Hochreiter 1991; Bengio, Simard and Frasconi 1994), so plain RNNs cannot learn dependencies more than a few steps long.

slides.title: LSTM: a memory with gates
slides.body:
![[fig-rnn-lstm|128%]]

> The memory is added to, not multiplied — so the signal can travel far.
slides.notes: The LSTM's answer: keep a second, separate memory — the belt on top — and change it only by adding. Three gates, each a small network with values between zero and one, decide: forget erases what is no longer needed, input writes what is new, output decides what the rest of the network gets to see. Along the belt the gradient is not squeezed at every step.
slides.summary: The LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997; the forget gate from Gers et al. 2000) keeps a separate cell state c that is changed by addition; three gates decide what to erase, what to write and what to read out, so gradients pass along c without vanishing.

slides.title: Attention: look back instead of carrying
slides.body:
![[fig-rnn-attention|128%]]

> Why carry everything, if you can look it up?
slides.notes: Then came a different idea: instead of squeezing everything into one state, let 'are' look back at every word and decide which ones matter — here, 'keys'. Attention started as help for recurrent translators in 2014; in 2017 the Transformer threw the recurrence away. The price: memory that grows with the length of the text.
slides.summary: Attention lets each word look back at every earlier word directly and weigh them (Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio 2014); the Transformer keeps only attention (Vaswani et al. 2017), trading the fixed-size state for memory that grows with the text.

slides.title: Recurrence returns
slides.body:
![[fig-rnn-timeline|128%]]

> Long contexts made the fixed-size state attractive again.
slides.notes: And now the loop is back. For very long inputs attention's growing memory hurts, and a fixed-size state looks good again. State-space models, Mamba, RWKV, xLSTM, even stripped-down 'minLSTM' — recurrent at heart, trained in parallel. The idea from 1990 still has legs.
slides.summary: From Elman's network (1990) and the LSTM (1997) through GRU, sequence-to-sequence models and attention (2014) to the Transformer (2017), and back: state-space models (S4, 2021), Mamba and RWKV (2023), xLSTM and minLSTM (2024) bring recurrence back for long sequences — linear time and a fixed-size state.

slides.title: Remember the loop
slides.body:
- **The state** carries what matters from word to word
- **Gradients** shrink or explode on the way back — **gates** let them through
- **Attention** looks back; **recurrence** carries forward — and is back

Further reading: Olah, *Understanding LSTM Networks* (2015) · Karpathy, *The Unreasonable Effectiveness of RNNs* (2015) · Goodfellow et al., *Deep Learning*, ch. 10
slides.notes: If you remember one picture, make it the loop. The rest is what happens when you try to train it, and what people built when it did not work. Read Chris Olah's post on LSTMs tonight — it is the best fifteen minutes on the topic.
slides.summary: Three things to remember — the state, the gradient's trouble and the gates, attention and the comeback of recurrence — with further reading.
